title: On What We Mean When We Say "Inclusive" Teaching
author: Rebecca Birch
summary: This article challenges the prevailing understanding of inclusive teaching, arguing that the dominant interpretation — which emphasises catering to individual uniqueness and diagnostic categories — is counterproductive and ultimately insulting to students with disabilities. Rebecca Birch, an Australian educator, points out that 27% of Australian students now have a disability and that systemic incentives around the NDIS and school funding have driven diagnostic inflation to the point where treating diverse learners as an 'individual needs' problem has become a practical impossibility. Her alternative: true inclusion means recognising that students with diverse learning profiles share the same fundamental cognitive architecture as everyone else, and therefore benefit from the same evidence-based practices — priming, clear explanations, predictability, safety, and guided practice — that benefit all learners. The article takes particular aim at personalised learning plans that specify obvious adjustments as though they were accommodations, arguing that the real barrier to inclusion is not lack of individualisation but lack of explicit, structured, high-quality teaching for everyone.
points: With 27% of Australian students now having a disability and diagnostic categories ballooning under funding incentives, treating inclusive education as an 'individual needs' differentiation problem has become a fool's errand destined to burn out the profession.

The core insight is that students with diverse learning profiles share the same fundamental cognitive architecture — they benefit from the same evidence-based practices (priming, clear explanations, predictability, guided practice) that benefit all learners.

Personalised learning plans that specify 'prime students for what's coming next, explain things, provide predictability' are not accommodations — they are basic good teaching, and framing them as special adjustments is a form of inadvertent condescension.

The dominant conception of inclusive teaching emphasises catering to uniqueness, when the research base points toward universal needs: even within diagnostic categories, students with ADHD or autism benefit from structured, explicit teaching practice.

The real language barrier to inclusion in Australian education is not reading and writing instruction but the professional discourse that equates inclusive teaching with individualised adaptation rather than high-quality whole-class explicit instruction.
quotes: Language might be the biggest barrier to Australian education meeting the needs of all. And I don't mean reading and writing. When I say 'inclusive,' I'm talking about full participation, ambitious curriculum, and the needs of the many being met.

27% of students in Australia have a disability, with many more imputed. The National Disability Insurance Scheme in Australia, and the current school funding model, have incentivised diagnosis. Diagnosis has bloomed like algae where the diagnostic categories and boundaries are less clear.
To treat this ballooning group of students as a differentiation or 'individual needs' issue is a fool's errand that will inevitably lead to the burnout of the profession.

Perhaps the issue is that common conceptions of inclusive teaching emphasise catering to uniqueness, rather than the universal needs and cognitive architecture that is highly similar between students. Even within diagnostic categories, and acknowledging diverse personalities and variance between students, I doubt that there are many students with ADHD or autism that don't benefit from things like priming, explanations, predictability, safety and guided practice.

I've been fighting for years against personalised learning plans for students with a disability that state the obvious as though it's an adjustment: 'Prime students for what's coming next, explain things, provide predictability, safety and guided practice.' I find them deeply insulting, but grudgingly acknowledge they are still necessary.

I'm yet to see a PLP that says, 'Prescribe a lot of group work, make your routines fresh and different each day, and let students explore their way out of complex problems.' Yet we still debate the adjustments we should make for diverse learners.
